title: What is spooking markets as stocks, Treasury yields and gold all fall ahead of European trading?
body: It looks like Halloween is coming a day early for markets with investors getting quite the fright already as we look to wrap up the trading week. Both stocks and Treasury yields are falling together, with gold also struggling to catch a bid. That's a rather spooky combination to deal with. So, what exactly is driving markets into this scary situation? Well, the latest earnings from Amazon overnight have only added another skeleton to the closet after the company's massive AI spending bill overshadowed impressive cloud growth. Amazon shares are down 7% in after-hours trading, and that follows from the beating that tech shares took yesterday after Alphabet reignited fears of AI spending in the day before. US futures are being dragged sharply lower today, with Nasdaq futures down 1.8% currently. And that is setting up a rather ominous backdrop ahead of European trading today. But beyond the selling in tech, there's something else about the broader market moves worth noting. Why are Treasury yields continuing to fall when inflation risks remain elevated? And why exactly aren't lower yields doing much to offer support for tech stocks? Perhaps the answer lies in the darker story brewing beneath the AI boom. For all the excitement surrounding AI technology, investors are starting to question just how much money companies need to throw at it before seeing meaningful returns. title: BOJ declares inflation victory but still won't budge on rates, so what's the hold-up?
body: If you think back to a decade ago, the BOJ being able to even see the path to reach the inflation target was very much a pipedream. Yet, here we are today. The central bank finally gets to declare victory on inflation. That must mean champagne all around, surely? Well, not quite. As it would seem, getting to the finish line and convincing policymakers to do something about it are two very different things. The BOJ kept its policy rate unchanged today at 1.25% in a 8-1 vote, with board member Takata dissenting in playing the role as the lone hawk again. He called for a 25 bps rate hike to 1.50% but the rest of the board wasn't having any of it. So, what's the story here? The most interesting bit of the meeting decision today is that the BOJ now says that underlying inflation has reached a level broadly consistent with its 2% target. Policymakers also expect inflation to remain around there as we move forward. So, that is quite a milestone after more than a decade of trying to get inflation sustainably back on track. Adding to that, the central bank also raised its core inflation forecast for fiscal year 2027 to 2.6% from 2.4% previously. So if inflation is already where policymakers want it to be, what's stopping them from moving faster? As it turns out, the overwhelming majority of the board clearly still prefers a more measured approach.

title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6548 – Reuters estimate
body: The People's Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point.

title: US employment cost index for Q3 +0.8% vs +0.8% expected
body: Prior quarter was +0.9% Employment benefits +0.9% vs +1.0% prior quarter Employment wages +0.7% vs +0.9% prior quarter The US Employment Cost Index (ECI) increased by 0.8% q/q in the third quarter, with both wages and salaries and benefit costs contributing to the increase. Wages and salaries rose 0.7%, while benefit costs increased 0.9% compared with the previous quarter. On an annual basis, total compensation costs for civilian workers increased by 3.4%, with wages and salaries rising 3.1% and benefit costs accelerating by 3.9%. The figures show that labour cost pressures remain relatively contained, although benefits continue to increase faster than wages. Looking at private industry, compensation costs also increased by 0.8% q/q and 3.4% y/y. However, inflation-adjusted wages and salaries declined by 0.6% over the year, as nominal wage growth is still failing to keep pace with consumer price increases. The continued gap between nominal and inflation-adjusted wage growth also highlights the pressure households are facing from higher living costs. For background, the Employment Cost Index (ECI) is a quarterly report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) that measures the change in the total cost of labor for businesses. The Fed considers the ECI the "gold standard" for measuring wage inflation because it is more precise and comprehensive, the only drawback is that it's not as timely as the Average Hourly Earnings data.

title: Ethereum tumbles as Binance hack triggers risk-off wave across crypto markets. What's next?
body: Ethereum tanked yesterday following the news of Binance security breach, which reportedly resulted in approximately $6.3 billion being drained from wallets across multiple blockchains. It was the largest cryptocurrency heist in history. The hack raised concerns about exchange security and potential contagion across the crypto ecosystem. Although Binance pledged to cover customer losses, uncertainty surrounding the stolen assets and potential liquidations weighed on sentiment. Around $1.53 billion in leveraged positions were liquidated over 24 hours. While the Binance hack triggered the initial shock, leveraged positioning and cascading liquidations magnified the losses. Historically, cryptocurrency selloffs triggered by exchange hacks have often been followed by a recovery, but the economic context decided how quickly. The initial reaction tends to be driven by panic, uncertainty and forced liquidations rather than a deterioration in the fundamentals of cryptocurrencies. The macro picture is still largely bearish given inflation risks, growth concerns, risk-off sentiment, upcoming rate hikes and geopolitical tensions. A significant improvement in risk sentiment is likely needed to change the current trend. Possible catalysts include a breakthrough in US-Iran negotiations and dovish Fed comments. title: Italy October preliminary CPI +5.4% vs +4.6% y/y expected
body: Prior +4.2% HICP +5.6% vs +4.6% y/y expected Prior +4.2% Inflation accelerated sharply in October 2026, but the increase was primarily driven by energy prices, with both regulated and non-regulated energy products recording significant increases. Regulated energy inflation surged from 25.8% to 59.5% y/y, while non-regulated energy prices accelerated from 22.5% to 29.4%. Higher energy costs remain the dominant driver of the inflationary shock. However, price pressures were not limited to energy. Unprocessed food inflation accelerated from 5.5% to 7.5%, while processed food prices also returned to positive annual growth. Services inflation picked up more modestly, rising to 2.9% from 2.6%, with transport-related services accelerating to 3.1%. The goods component was particularly notable, with annual inflation jumping to 7.5% from 5.4%, while services inflation remained considerably more contained. This suggests that the latest acceleration is still heavily concentrated in goods and energy-related costs rather than reflecting an equally broad-based increase across the services sector. Overall, the data points to significant inflationary shock in Italy, largely driven by surging energy costs but increasingly spilling over into food and transportation prices. This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

title: Eurozone Q3 GDP beats expectations but the growth surprise comes with a catch
body: Eurozone Q3 preliminary GDP +0.4% vs +0.2% q/q expected Prior +0.6% Eurozone Q3 preliminary GDP +1.3% vs +1.1% y/y expected Prior +1.2% Well, well, well. Would you look at that. The euro area economy has managed to pull a rabbit out of the hat, delivering a better-than-expected Q3 GDP reading at first glance. But before we start popping the champagne, there's a catch or two worth considering when you look at the details. To start, quarterly growth did still slow down to 0.4% in the third quarter - down from 0.6% in the second quarter. So while the headline surprise is encouraging, the underlying momentum isn't quite as impressive as it might seem. And when you drill deeper into the details, that is when things start to get a bit more interesting. Of note, Ireland leads the pack with a whopping 5.5% quarterly expansion in Q3. Having said that, Ireland has a knack for notoriously volatile GDP figures in the past year and that always warrants some caution. The expansion here was primarily driven by strong activity in multinational-dominated industries, specifically information and communication and manufacturing. For some context, Ireland's headline growth figure is often a distorted gauge of domestic economic health. That is because it is heavily influenced by contract manufacturing and global profits of multinational corporations that largely flow back to foreign shareholders rather than translating directly into local living standards.

title: German state inflation cools in October, but will that ease the ECB's headache?
body: The state readings released around the same time: Bavaria September CPI +2.8% vs +3.2% y/y prior Saxony September CPI +2.9% vs +3.3% y/y prior North Rhine Westphalia September CPI +2.7% vs +3.3% y/y prior Baden Wuerttemberg September CPI +2.6% vs +2.9% y/y prior After the acceleration in September, headline inflation is seen cooling back a little in German states. While base effects are part of the reason, the re-implementation of specific energy tax reductions and fuel discounts enacted at the start of the month are arguably also playing a part here. So, that is leading to cooler price pressures overall but still relatively elevated when compared to the months before this. Putting the estimates together, it offers an indication that German inflation is set to decline at the national level as well. Headline annual inflation is expected to drop to 3.0% in October from 3.3% last month, with the state readings above pointing to a modest likelihood that we might even see a reading below the 3% mark. In any case, just keep in mind though that the state readings aren't a perfect proxy for the national figure. There can still be some deviation when the preliminary numbers are released later. However, they have historically been a useful gauge and today's readings arguably point to some downside risk to the 3.0% consensus, with a national CPI reading around 2.9% now looking quite plausible.

title: Italy Q3 preliminary GDP +0.0% vs +0.1% q/q expected
body: Prior +0.2% GDP Y/Y +0.8% vs +0.9% y/y expected Prior +1.0% Italy's economy unexpectedly stalled in the third quarter of 2026, with GDP remaining unchanged q/q, following 0.2% growth in the previous quarter. On an annual basis, GDP increased by 0.8%, pointing to a relatively modest pace of economic expansion. On the supply side, services and agriculture provided positive contributions to growth, while industrial activity declined. The weakness in industry remains a concern, particularly given the sector's importance to Italy's export-oriented economy. On the demand side, domestic demand, including changes in inventories, supported economic activity, while net foreign demand acted as a drag. This suggests that domestic spending continues to provide some resilience, but external demand and trade flows remain a source of weakness. The carry-over growth rate for 2026 stands at 0.8% on a calendar-adjusted basis. This means that even if GDP remains unchanged in the fourth quarter, annual growth would still be around 0.8%, although the final annual figure may differ due to the three additional working days in 2026 compared with 2025. The report is mildly negative for the growth outlook. The stagnation in quarterly GDP, combined with industrial weakness and a negative contribution from net exports, highlights structural growth challenges. Domestic demand remains the main source of resilience, but the economy is still struggling to generate broader-based growth.

title: Germany Q3 preliminary GDP +0.2% vs +0.1% q/q expected
body: Prior +0.3% GDP Y/Y +1.2% vs 1.1% expected Prior +1.0% Germany's economy expanded by 0.2% q/q in the third quarter of 2026, according to preliminary data from Destatis, extending the recovery seen in the first half of the year. GDP increased by 1.3% y/y in price-adjusted terms, or 1.2% when adjusted for both prices and calendar effects. However, the underlying details point to a loss of momentum, with the recovery becoming increasingly uneven. Consumer spending made a modest positive contribution, suggesting that domestic demand is holding up, but investment declined, highlighting continued weakness in business activity. Meanwhile, exports, which provided a significant boost to growth during the first half of the year, lost momentum in Q3. This is particularly relevant for Germany, given its heavy reliance on external demand and the importance of its manufacturing and export sectors. Overall, the report suggests that Germany's economic recovery is losing some steam. Growth is still positive, although the weaker performance of investment and exports raises questions about how sustainable the recovery will be heading into the final quarter of the year considering all the headwinds from tightening financial conditions and geopolitical shocks. This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

title: Gold gets hit again by forced liquidations as equity losses mount; fundamental outlook increasingly positive
body: Gold came under renewed pressure yesterday as another selloff in equities weighed on precious metals. Gold has been tightly correlated with the stock market recently, with the latest losses seemingly driven by investors liquidating positions to cover losses elsewhere in their portfolios. Chart: You can see the correlation between the Nasdaq (blue line) and gold (candlesticks) To understand the mechanics, imagine that an investment fund holds stocks, gold and government bonds. Some stocks suddenly crash, and the fund suffers losses on leveraged positions. The fund may need to raise cash to meet margin calls, reduce leverage or satisfy investor redemptions. Rather than selling only the assets that caused the losses, it may sell whatever it can liquidate quickly. Gold is particularly useful in this situation because it is highly liquid and can be sold quickly. The main drivers like real yields have been actually pointing to higher gold prices. In fact, real yields fell significantly as inflation expectations remain roughly unchanged given the increase in oil prices, while nominal Treasury yields fell as the losses in the stock market triggered a flight to safety. We can also see the unusual divergence between spot gold and the ETFs holdings in the chart below. Generally speaking, spot prices lead ETFs inflows and outflows, but in this case, I think it's technical factors capping the upside in gold, not fundamental ones.

title: Spain Q3 GDP growth slows slightly but it's the inflation problem that should worry the ECB
body: Spain Q3 preliminary GDP +0.6% vs +0.6% q/q expected Prior +0.7% Spain Q3 preliminary GDP +2.7% vs +2.7% y/y expected Prior +2.6% It is the preliminary report, so there aren't much details to work with here besides the headline figures above. The quarterly figure does show a bit of a slowdown in Spanish economic growth in the third quarter, albeit marginally. And among the bigger names in the euro area, Spain is still very much punching above its weight in carrying the more optimistic banner for the region. The only issue is that inflation pressures in Spain is also starting to get out of hand. Headline annual inflation is bordering on 5% in October with core annual inflation holding above 3%. Those numbers are way beyond what the ECB would be comfortable with, running above their 2% price target. The Spanish GDP report here isn't something to spook markets. But a mild slowdown if coupled with troubling performances in France and perhaps Germany later, that could really ramp up talk of stagflation risks in the euro area especially when paired with the inflation numbers today. Traders might still lean more favourably on inflation risks prompting the ECB to act in December. But if growth conditions continue to suffer, it might only be a matter of time before the narrative shifts and the focus turns to stagflation risks instead. So, just be wary of that. This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

title: Spain inflation remains stubbornly high near 5% as the ECB headache gets worse
body: Spain October preliminary CPI +4.9% vs +4.9% y/y expected Prior +4.9% Spain October preliminary HICP +4.9% vs +4.9% y/y expected Prior +5.0% Spanish inflation continues to hover around 5% in October, as the preliminary estimates continue to paint a rather uncomfortable picture for the most part. Headline annual inflation remains steady at 4.9% while the harmonised reading eased marginally to 4.9% as well. So, that's not saying a lot after the run higher in the past few months amid a surge energy prices due to the Middle East conflict. And with higher oil prices continuing to stick, that will certainly add to the inflation headache in Q4. Looking at the details, core annual inflation is seen at 3.1% - unchanged compared to September. But at this level, it is still well above what the ECB would be comfortable with as price pressures continue to pull away from the 2% target. Alongside the earlier report from France, this just continues to reaffirm that the inflation monster is getting bigger and more threatening for the central bank. But at the same time, flagging economic growth conditions will just mean that stagflation risks are also on the rise. So, that is quite a troubling spot for policymakers to be in as they have to try and deal with price pressures before they get out of hand while avoiding sending the broader economy off a cliff. Tough. This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

title: France inflation heats up again in October, leaving the ECB caught between a rock and a hard place
body: France October preliminary CPI +3.4% vs +3.2% y/y expected Prior +3.1% France October preliminary HICP +3.8% vs +3.6% y/y expected Prior +3.4% French inflation is seen accelerating again in October, as the preliminary estimates show headline annual inflation climbing to its highest since December 2023. Yowza. The main culprit is once again energy prices, as that continues to fuel much of the headline price increase. No pun intended. Of note, energy price inflation was up 24.1% annually in October compared to 21.3% in the month before. The detailed breakdown shows food price inflation softening slightly to 1.2% in October but services inflation is seen picking up further to 2.7% from 2.4% in the month before. The latter is a real issue as it signals that higher energy prices are starting to spill over more broadly, and that will in turn feed into core inflation as well. It's not a good look if you're the ECB. France is already struggling economically, not to mention with fiscal headwinds growing stronger by the day. And with inflation pressures starting to heat up as well, that is making for a very stagflationary outlook for Europe's second-largest economy. For the central bank, this is their biggest issue and risk to tightening policy further. That is especially the case as French bonds are also coming under heavy pressure amid fiscal worries and that could threaten to blow over to the rest of the euro area as well.

title: German import prices surge at fastest pace in nearly four years as energy costs bite
body: Germany September import prices +2.1% vs +1.8% m/m expected Prior +1.0% Germany September import prices +10.4% vs +10.3% y/y expected Prior +8.3% Just when Germany thought it had enough economic headaches to deal with, here's another one to add to the pile. This time, the inflation monster is making quite the comeback through the back door. German import prices for September are seen rosing at their fastest annual pace since November 2022, with the monthly increase also coming in hotter than expected. And surprise, surprise. Not. It is energy that is once again doing much of the damage.
